_readme: Curated knowledge base for Nemo Care's Insights engine. Each parameter has low/high state entries (normal states generally produce no insight, so are omitted unless noted). Each entry is deliberately conservative and uses associative language ('may', 'associated with') rather than diagnostic claims — this is intentional and should be preserved by the insight writer agent. 'sourceOrganizations' names the general body whose guidelines back the claim; before shipping, replace with a specific cited URL (use the KB curator agent + Tavily to fetch one, then have a human approve it, as per the original design). ageConsiderations and recommendedFollowUpTests are the fields the findings engine + insight writer use most directly for the Glaucoma-style example.

high.severityNote: Distinguish borderline (prediabetic range) from clearly elevated — severity changes urgency of language.
commonCauses: Insulin resistance or early/established type 2 diabetes
High-carbohydrate diet combined with low physical activity
possibleEffects: Increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue
Blurred vision
Slow-healing cuts or frequent infections
Over years: damage to blood vessels and nerves (diabetic complications)

ageConsiderations.note: Long-standing elevated glucose is associated with a higher risk of diabetic retinopathy and a modestly increased risk of glaucoma and cataracts, due to chronic damage to small blood vessels in the eye.
Associated with higher risk of peripheral neuropathy (numbness/tingling in feet) with longer duration of elevated glucose.
Associated with increased cardiovascular risk, compounding with other risk factors like high cholesterol or high blood pressure.

recommendedFollowUpTests: HbA1c (if only random/fasting glucose was tested) — shows 3-month average
Lipid profile — diabetes and high cholesterol often co-occur
Kidney function test (creatinine, eGFR, urine microalbumin) — screens for diabetic kidney involvement
Dilated eye exam — screens for diabetic retinopathy, especially if duration is unclear or age 40+
Foot sensation exam (if numbness/tingling reported)
generalLifestyleNotes: Post-meal short walks (10-15 min) are commonly associated with lower post-meal glucose spikes
Reducing refined sugar and simple carbohydrate intake
Regular physical activity and weight management where applicable

low.severityNote: A single low reading from random testing is often less significant than a pattern; recurrent lows in a non-diabetic person warrant attention.
commonCauses: Excess diabetes medication/insulin relative to food intake (if on treatment)
Intense exercise without adequate food intake
possibleEffects: Shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion
Palpitations
In severe cases: loss of consciousness (medical emergency)

ageConsiderations.note: Older adults may have blunted symptoms of low blood sugar, making recurrent lows more likely to go unnoticed and increasing fall risk.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Repeat fasting glucose to confirm pattern vs one-off reading
Review of current medications if on diabetes treatment
HbA1c for overall glucose control context
generalLifestyleNotes: If on diabetes medication, discuss dosing with a doctor rather than self-adjusting

high.severityNote: Stage matters: 130-139/80-89 (stage 1) vs 140+/90+ (stage 2) vs 180+/120+ (hypertensive crisis — needs urgent care, not a routine insight).
commonCauses: Essential (primary) hypertension — often multifactorial: genetics, diet (high sodium), weight, stress
Certain medications (NSAIDs, decongestants, some birth control)
possibleEffects: Often asymptomatic ("silent") in early stages
Headaches, in more severe elevation
Over years: increased risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney damage, vision changes

ageConsiderations.note: Associated with higher risk of hypertensive retinopathy (blood vessel changes in the eye) and increased cardiovascular and stroke risk with longer duration of uncontrolled hypertension.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Repeat BP measurement on multiple occasions (single reading is not diagnostic)
Kidney function test (creatinine, urea)
Lipid profile
ECG, especially if symptoms present
Eye exam if longstanding/uncontrolled

commonCauses: Certain medications (blood pressure meds, some antidepressants)
Some individuals have naturally low baseline BP with no issue
possibleEffects: Dizziness or lightheadedness, especially on standing
Fatigue
In severe cases: fainting

ageConsiderations.note: Associated with higher fall risk due to orthostatic (postural) drops in blood pressure.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Orthostatic BP check (lying vs standing)
Review of current medications
Thyroid function test

high.severityNote: Correlate with eGFR if available — a more direct kidney function measure than creatinine alone.
commonCauses: Reduced kidney function (acute or chronic kidney disease)
High-protein diet or intense muscle exertion (transient)
Longstanding uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension (leading causes of chronic kidney disease)
possibleEffects: Often asymptomatic until significantly elevated
Fatigue, swelling (edema), changes in urination with more advanced reduction in kidney function

ageConsiderations.note: Particularly relevant if the patient also has high blood sugar or high blood pressure — these together are the leading causes of progressive kidney function decline.

recommendedFollowUpTests: eGFR (often calculated automatically alongside creatinine)
Urine microalbumin/protein test
Blood urea / BUN
Electrolytes (potassium, sodium)
Repeat test after ensuring adequate hydration, to rule out a transient cause

commonCauses: Heart failure (reduced blood flow to kidneys)
possibleEffects: Often correlates with symptoms related to its underlying cause rather than urea itself
recommendedFollowUpTests: Creatinine and eGFR together for a fuller kidney function picture
Hydration status review

possibleEffects: Usually not significant in isolation

commonCauses: Diet high in purines (red meat, organ meat, certain seafood, alcohol especially beer)
Reduced kidney excretion of uric acid
possibleEffects: Gout — sudden, severe joint pain and swelling, classically in the big toe
Uric acid kidney stones
Often asymptomatic ("hyperuricemia") without ever causing gout

ageConsiderations.note: Risk of gout flare-ups and kidney stone formation increases with longstanding elevated uric acid.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Kidney function test (creatinine, eGFR) — elevated uric acid and reduced kidney function often occur together
Joint exam if any joint pain/swelling present
generalLifestyleNotes: Reducing purine-rich foods and alcohol (especially beer)

possibleEffects: Usually not clinically significant on its own

high.severityNote: Even trace/mild proteinuria in a patient with diabetes or hypertension is clinically meaningful and worth flagging prominently — it's an early kidney-involvement signal.
commonCauses: Early kidney involvement from diabetes or high blood pressure
possibleEffects: Often no symptoms at mild levels
Foamy urine, swelling (edema) at higher levels
Early marker of kidney damage, particularly important for patients with diabetes or hypertension
recommendedFollowUpTests: Repeat urine test to confirm (not a one-off cause like exercise/fever)
Urine microalbumin-to-creatinine ratio (more precise than dipstick)
Kidney function test (creatinine, eGFR)
Blood pressure and blood glucose review, since both are common underlying drivers

possibleEffects: Usually asymptomatic
Over years: contributes to atherosclerosis (plaque buildup in arteries), raising risk of heart attack and stroke

ageConsiderations.note: Cardiovascular risk from elevated LDL compounds significantly with age, smoking status, and other risk factors like high blood sugar or high blood pressure.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Full lipid profile (LDL, HDL, triglycerides) if only total cholesterol was tested
Blood glucose/HbA1c — cholesterol and glucose abnormalities often co-occur
Thyroid function test (TSH) — hypothyroidism can elevate cholesterol
ECG or cardiac risk assessment if multiple risk factors present

possibleEffects: Low HDL alone is usually asymptomatic but is an independent cardiovascular risk factor, especially combined with high LDL or triglycerides
recommendedFollowUpTests: Full lipid profile for complete risk picture
Blood glucose/HbA1c
generalLifestyleNotes: Regular aerobic exercise is one of the more consistently effective ways to raise HDL

commonCauses: High intake of sugar and refined carbohydrates
possibleEffects: Usually asymptomatic
Very high levels (severely elevated) can rarely cause pancreatitis
Contributes to cardiovascular risk, especially combined with low HDL and high LDL (a common combination called atherogenic dyslipidemia)
recommendedFollowUpTests: Full lipid profile
Blood glucose/HbA1c — strong link with insulin resistance
Liver function test — fatty liver often co-occurs with high triglycerides
generalLifestyleNotes: Reducing sugar, refined carbs, and alcohol

commonCauses: Chronic blood loss (heavy menstrual periods, GI bleeding)
possibleEffects: Fatigue, weakness
Shortness of breath on exertion
Pale skin, cold hands/feet
Brittle nails, hair thinning
Restless legs, in some cases
recommendedFollowUpTests: Complete Blood Count (hemoglobin, MCV, MCH) if not already done — iron deficiency classically shows low MCV/MCH
Ferritin specifically (a more direct marker of iron stores than serum iron alone)
Investigation of source if chronic blood loss suspected (e.g. heavy periods, GI evaluation)

possibleEffects: Fatigue, joint pain
Over years: potential liver, heart, or pancreas involvement if untreated
recommendedFollowUpTests: Repeat ferritin and transferrin saturation
Liver function test
Genetic testing for hemochromatosis, if pattern suggests it

possibleEffects: Muscle cramps or twitches
Fatigue despite adequate sleep duration
Poor sleep quality
In more significant deficiency: irregular heartbeat, numbness/tingling
recommendedFollowUpTests: Calcium and potassium levels — these electrolytes often move together
Kidney function test

commonCauses: Excessive magnesium supplement or antacid use
possibleEffects: Often asymptomatic at mild elevation
Nausea, muscle weakness at higher levels
recommendedFollowUpTests: Kidney function test (creatinine, eGFR)

possibleEffects: Muscle cramps, tingling around mouth/fingers
Over years: contributes to reduced bone density
recommendedFollowUpTests: Vitamin D level — frequently the underlying cause
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) level if low calcium persists
Kidney function test

possibleEffects: Fatigue, constipation
Increased thirst and urination
Kidney stones with prolonged elevation
recommendedFollowUpTests: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) level
Kidney function test
Vitamin D level

commonCauses: Diet low in vitamin D-rich foods
Obesity (vitamin D is sequestered in fat tissue)
possibleEffects: Fatigue, low mood
Bone/muscle aches
Over years: contributes to reduced bone density, increased fracture risk
Associated with lower calcium absorption, compounding bone health effects
recommendedFollowUpTests: Calcium level
Bone density scan (DEXA) if risk factors for osteoporosis present, especially in older adults
generalLifestyleNotes: Dietary sources: fatty fish, fortified foods

commonCauses: Vegetarian/vegan diet without supplementation (B12 is mainly found in animal products)
Long-term use of certain medications (e.g. metformin, acid-reducing drugs)
possibleEffects: Fatigue, weakness
Numbness/tingling in hands or feet
Memory difficulties, mood changes
In combination with low iron: compounded fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance

ageConsiderations.note: Age-related reduced stomach acid can impair B12 absorption even with adequate dietary intake, making deficiency more common in older adults.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Complete Blood Count (B12 deficiency can cause macrocytic — large RBC — anemia, the opposite pattern from iron deficiency)
Folate level (often tested alongside B12)
Methylmalonic acid (MMA), in cases of borderline B12 with symptoms, for more sensitive detection

possibleEffects: Fatigue, weakness
Shortness of breath on exertion
Pale skin, dizziness
Reduced exercise tolerance
recommendedFollowUpTests: MCV/MCH (from the same CBC) to narrow down the likely cause — low MCV suggests iron deficiency, high MCV suggests B12/folate deficiency
Ferritin and iron studies
Vitamin B12 and folate levels
Investigation of blood loss source if indicated by history

commonCauses: Dehydration (relative concentration, not a true increase)
Lung or heart conditions causing chronically low oxygen
possibleEffects: Often asymptomatic
Headaches, dizziness, in more significant elevation
Increased risk of blood clots at very high levels
recommendedFollowUpTests: Repeat test after ensuring adequate hydration
Oxygen saturation (SpO2)
Review of smoking history

low.severityNote: Both MCV and MCH below reference together form a microcytic / hypochromic pattern. Interpret with the latest CBC only.
possibleEffects: Often linked educationally with iron-deficiency anemia patterns
Fatigue or reduced exercise tolerance when hemoglobin is also low
recommendedFollowUpTests: Ferritin and iron studies
Review hemoglobin trend on the same CBC
Discuss with a clinician before starting iron supplements
generalLifestyleNotes: Iron-rich foods may be discussed when clinically appropriate
Do not self-start high-dose iron without medical advice

high.severityNote: A high neutrophil percentage is a lab pattern, not a diagnosis. Correlate with symptoms and absolute counts.
possibleEffects: Often reflects the body's response to illness or stress
Persistent elevation may warrant clinical correlation
recommendedFollowUpTests: Repeat CBC if unexpected
Clinical review for fever, recent illness, or medications

combinations.title: Elevated blood sugar and cholesterol together
combinations.combinedRisk: This combination is a recognized pattern (often part of what's called metabolic syndrome) and is associated with meaningfully higher cardiovascular risk than either finding alone, plus an increased likelihood of fatty liver disease.
possibleEffects: Higher combined risk of heart attack and stroke than either factor individually
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is commonly associated with this combination
Accelerated blood vessel damage, compounding risk to eyes, kidneys, and nerves
recommendedFollowUpTests: Liver function test (fatty liver screening)
HbA1c for glucose control overview
Full lipid profile (LDL, HDL, triglycerides) if not already complete
ECG or cardiac risk assessment
Waist circumference / BMI as part of metabolic syndrome criteria

combinations.title: Elevated blood sugar in patients 45 and older
combinations.combinedRisk: Longer probable duration of elevated glucose in this age group raises the relevance of eye, kidney, and nerve screening, since diabetic complications develop over years.
possibleEffects: Higher associated risk of diabetic retinopathy and, less directly, glaucoma and cataracts
Higher associated risk of diabetic kidney involvement
Higher associated risk of peripheral neuropathy
recommendedFollowUpTests: Dilated eye exam
Urine microalbumin test
Foot sensation exam

combinations.title: Reduced kidney function with elevated blood pressure
combinations.combinedRisk: These two commonly reinforce each other — reduced kidney function can raise blood pressure, and uncontrolled blood pressure accelerates kidney function decline — making this combination worth closer monitoring than either alone.
possibleEffects: Faster progression of chronic kidney disease if blood pressure remains uncontrolled
Increased cardiovascular risk
recommendedFollowUpTests: eGFR trend over time (not just a single reading)
Urine microalbumin/protein test
Electrolyte panel

combinations.title: Low iron and low magnesium together
combinations.combinedRisk: Both deficiencies independently cause fatigue through different mechanisms (reduced oxygen-carrying capacity vs muscle/nerve and sleep-quality effects), so together they are commonly associated with more pronounced tiredness than either alone — including feeling unrested even after adequate sleep duration.
possibleEffects: Persistent fatigue despite sufficient sleep hours
Muscle cramps combined with reduced exercise tolerance
Poor sleep quality contributing further to daytime tiredness
recommendedFollowUpTests: Ferritin and full iron studies
Magnesium and calcium levels
Review of diet for both nutrients

combinations.title: Elevated uric acid with reduced kidney function
combinations.combinedRisk: Reduced kidney function lowers uric acid excretion, often elevating it further, while elevated uric acid itself can contribute to kidney stone formation — a self-reinforcing pattern worth monitoring together.
possibleEffects: Higher risk of gout flare-ups
Higher risk of uric acid kidney stones
recommendedFollowUpTests: eGFR trend
Joint exam if any pain/swelling present
Kidney ultrasound if stone symptoms present

combinations.title: Low calcium and low vitamin D together
combinations.combinedRisk: Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption, so these two commonly occur together and compound each other's effect on bone health over time.
possibleEffects: Increased risk of reduced bone density and fractures over time
Muscle cramps and bone/muscle aches

ageConsiderations.note: This combination is particularly relevant for bone density screening in postmenopausal women and older adults generally.

recommendedFollowUpTests: Bone density scan (DEXA), especially in postmenopausal women or adults 50+
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) level

combinations.title: Low hemoglobin with low vitamin B12
combinations.combinedRisk: B12 deficiency is itself a cause of anemia (typically with large red blood cells/high MCV), so this combination points toward B12 deficiency as a likely contributor to the low hemoglobin, rather than two unrelated findings.
possibleEffects: Compounded fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance
Neurological symptoms (numbness/tingling, memory difficulty) in addition to anemia symptoms
recommendedFollowUpTests: MCV from the CBC — high MCV supports a B12/folate-related cause
Folate level
Methylmalonic acid (MMA) if B12 is borderline
